sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.stage: SCENE: —The Orchestra represents the Pnyx at Athens; in the background is the house of Demos.
sp.p: Oh! alas! alas! Oh! woe! oh! woe! Miserable Paphlagonian! may the gods destroy both him and his cursed advice! Since that evil day when this new slave entered the house he has never ceased belaboring us with blows.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: May the plague seize him, the arch-fiend —him and his lying tales!

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Hah! my poor fellow, what is your condition?

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Very wretched, just like your own.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Then come, let us sing a duet of groans in the style of Olympus.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes and Nicias
sp.p: Boo, hoo! boo, hoo! boo, hoo! boo, hoo! boo, hoo! boo, hoo!!

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Bah! it's lost labour to weep! Enough of groaning! Let us consider how to save our pelts.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: But how to do it! Can you suggest anything?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: No, you begin.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: I cede you the honor.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: By Apollo! no, not I

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: “Ah! would you but tell me what I should tell you!”

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Come, have courage! Speak, and then I will say what I think.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: I dare not. How could I express my thoughts with the pomp of Euripides?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Oh! please spare me! Do not pelt me with those vegetables, but find some way of leaving our master.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Well, then! Say “Let-us-bolt,” like this, in one breath.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: I follow you —“Let-us-bolt.”

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Now after “Let-us-bolt” say “at-top-speed!”

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: “At-top-speed!”

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Splendid! Just as if you were masturbating; first slowly, “Let-us-bolt”; then quick and firmly, “at-top-speed!”

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Let-us-bolt, let-us-bolt-at-top-speed!

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Hah! does that not please you?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Yes, indeed, yet I fear your omen bodes no good to my hide.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: How so?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Because masturbation chafes the skin.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: The best thing we can do for the moment is to throw ourselves at the feet of the statue of some god.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Of which statue? Any statue? Do you then believe there are gods?

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Certainly.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: What proof have you?

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: The proof that they have taken a grudge against me. Is that not enough?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: I'm convinced it is. But to pass on. Do you consent to my telling the spectators of our troubles?

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: There's nothing wrong with that, and we might ask them to show us by their manner, whether our facts and actions are to their liking.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: I will begin then. We have a very brutal master, a perfect glutton for beans, and most bad-tempered; it's Demos of the Pnyx, an intolerable old man and half deaf. The beginning of last month he bought a slave, a Paphlagonian tanner, an arrant rogue, the incarnation of calumny. This man of leather knows his old master thoroughly; he plays the fawning cur, flatters, cajoles, wheedles, and dupes him at will with little scraps of leavings, which he allows him to get. “Dear Demos,” he will say, “try a single case and you will have done enough; then take your bath, eat, swallow and devour; here are three obols.” Then the Paphlagonian filches from one of us what we have prepared and makes a present of it to our old man. The other day I had just kneaded a Spartan cake at Pylos, the cunning rogue came behind my back, sneaked it and offered the cake, which was my invention, in his own name. He keeps us at a distance and suffers none but himself to wait upon the master; when Demos is dining, he keeps close to his side with a thong in his hand and puts the orators to flight. He keeps singing oracles to him, so that the old man now thinks of nothing but the Sibyl. Then, when he sees him thoroughly obfuscated, he uses all his cunning and piles up lies and calumnies against the household; then we are scourged and the Paphlagonian runs about among the slaves to demand contributions with threats and gathers them in with both hands. He will say, “You see how I have had Hylas beaten! Either content me or die at once!” We are forced to give, for otherwise the old man tramples on us and makes us crap forth all our body contains. To Nicias There must be an end to it, friend. Let us see! what can be done? Who will get us out of this mess?

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: The best thing, friend, is our famous “Let-us-bolt!”

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: But none can escape the Paphlagonian, his eye is everywhere. And what a stride! He has one leg on Pylos and the other in the Assembly; his arse gapes exactly over the land of the Chaonians, his hands are with the Aetolians and his mind with the Clopidians.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: It's best then to die; but let us seek the most heroic death.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Let me think, what is the most heroic?

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Let us drink the blood of a bull; that's the death Themistocles chose.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: No, not that, but a bumper of good unmixed wine in honor of the Good Genius; perchance we may stumble on a happy thought.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Look at him! “Unmixed wine!” Your mind is on drink intent? Can a man strike out a brilliant thought when drunk?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Without question. Go, ninny, blow yourself out with water; do you dare to accuse wine of clouding the reason? Quote me more marvellous effects than those of wine. Look! when a man drinks, he is rich, everything he touches succeeds, he gains lawsuits, is happy and helps his friends. Come, bring hither quick a flagon of wine, that I may soak my brain and get an ingenious idea.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: My God! What can your drinking do to help us?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Much. But bring it to me, while I take my seat. Once drunk, I shall strew little ideas, little phrases, little reasonings everywhere.

div.stage: Nicias enters the house and returns almost immediately with a bottle.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: It is lucky I was not caught in the house stealing the wine.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Tell me, what is the Paphlagonian doing now?

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: The wretch has just gobbled up some confiscated cakes; he is drunk and lies at full-length snoring on his hides.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Very well, come along, pour me out wine and plenty of it.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Take it and offer a libation to your Good Genius.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Inhale, ah, inhale the spirit of the genius of Pramnium.
Ah! Good Genius, thine the plan, not mine!

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Tell me, what is it?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Run indoors quick and steal the oracles of the Paphlagonian, while he is asleep.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Bless me! I fear this Good Genius will be but a very Bad Genius for me.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: And I'll set the flagon near me, that I may moisten my wit to invent some brilliant notion.

div.stage: Nicias enters the house and returns at once.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: How loudly the Paphlagonian farts and snores! I was able to seize the sacred oracle, which he was guarding with the greatest care, without his seeing me.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Oh! clever fellow! Hand it here, that I may read. Come, pour me out some drink, bestir yourself! Let me see what there is in it. Oh! prophecy! Some drink! some drink! Quick!

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Well! what says the oracle?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Pour again.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Is “pour again” in the oracle?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Oh, Bacis!

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: But what is in it?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Quick! some drink!

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Bacis is very dry!

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Oh! miserable Paphlagonian! This then is why you have so long taken such precautions; your horoscope gave you qualms of terror.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: What does it say?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: It says here how he must end.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: And how?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: How? the oracle announces clearly that a dealer in oakum must first govern the city.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: That's one tradesman. And after him, who?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: After him, a sheep-dealer.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Two tradesmen, eh? And what is this one's fate?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: To reign until a filthier scoundrel than he arises; then he perishes and in his place the leather-seller appears, the Paphlagonian robber, the bawler, who roars like a torrent.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: And the leather-seller must destroy the sheep-seller?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Oh! woe is me! Where can another seller be found, is there ever a one left?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: There is yet one, who plies a first-rate trade.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Tell me, pray, what is that?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: You really want to know?

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Well then! it's a sausage-seller who must overthrow him.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: A sausage-seller! Ah! by Poseidon! what a fine trade! But where can this man be found?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Let's seek him.

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: But look! there he is, going towards the market-place; 'tis the gods, the gods who send him!

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Calling out.This way, this way, oh, lucky sausage-seller, come forward, dear friend, our saviour, the saviour of our city.

div.stage: Enter Sausage-Seller carrying a basket of his wares.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: What is it? Why do you call me?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Come here, come and learn about your good luck, you who are Fortune's favorite!

sp.speaker: Nicias
sp.p: Come! Relieve him of his basket-tray and tell him the oracle of the god; I will go and look after the Paphlagonian.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: First put down all your gear, then worship the earth and the gods.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Done. What is the matter?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Happiness, riches, power; to-day you have nothing, to-morrow you will have all, oh! chief of happy Athens.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Why not leave me to wash my tripe and to sell my sausages instead of making game of me?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Oh! the fool! Your tripe! Do you see these tiers of people?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: You shall be master to them all, governor of the market, of the harbors, of the Pnyx; you shall trample the Senate under foot, be able to cashier the generals, load them with fetters, throw them into gaol, and you will fornicate in the Prytaneum.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: What! I?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: You, without a doubt. But you do not yet see all the glory awaiting you. Stand on your basket and look at all the islands that surround Athens.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I see them. What then?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Look at the storehouses and the shipping.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Yes, I am looking.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Exists there a mortal more blest than you? Furthermore, turn your right eye towards Caria and your left toward Carthage!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Then it's a blessing to be cock-eyed!

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: No, but you are the one who is going to trade away all this. According to the oracle you must become the greatest of men.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Just tell me how a sausage-seller can become a great man.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: That is precisely why you will be great, because you are a sad rascal without shame, no better than a common market rogue.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I do not hold myself worthy of wielding power.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Oh! by the gods! Why do you not hold yourself worthy? Have you then such a good opinion of yourself? Come, are you of honest parentage?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: By the gods! No! of very bad indeed.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Spoilt child of fortune, everything fits together to ensure your greatness.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: But I have not had the least education. I can only read, and that very badly.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: That is what may stand in your way, almost knowing how to read. A demagogue must be neither an educated nor an honest man; he has to be an ignoramus and a rogue. But do not, do not let go this gift, which the oracle promises.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: But what does the oracle say?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Faith, it is put together in very fine enigmatical style, as elegant as it is clear:

“When the eagle-tanner with the hooked claws shall seize a stupid dragon, a blood-sucker, it will be an end to the hot Paphlagonian pickled garlic. The god grants great glory to the sausage-sellers unless they prefer to sell their wares.”

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: In what way does this concern me? Please instruct my ignorance.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: The eagle-tanner is the Paphlagonian.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: What do the hooked claws mean?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: It means to say, that he robs and pillages us with his claw-like hands.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And the dragon?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: That is quite clear. The dragon is long and so also is the sausage; the sausage like the dragon is a drinker of blood. Therefore the oracle says, that the dragon will triumph over the eagle-tanner, if he does not let himself be cajoled with words.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: The oracles of the gods flatter me! Faith! I do not at all understand how I can be capable of governing the people.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Nothing simpler. Continue your trade. Mix and knead together all the state business as you do for your sausages. To win the people, always cook them some savoury that pleases them. Besides, you possess all the attributes of a demagogue; a screeching, horrible voice, a perverse, crossgrained nature and the language of the market-place. In you all is united which is needful for governing. The oracles are in your favour, even including that of Delphi. Come, take a chaplet, offer a libation to the god of Stupidity and take care to fight vigorously.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Who will be my ally? for the rich fear the Paphlagonian and the poor shudder at the sight of him.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: You will have a thousand brave Knights, who detest him, on your side; also the honest citizens amongst the spectators, those who are men of brave hearts, and finally myself and the god. Fear not, you will not see his features, for none have dared to make a mask resembling him. But the public have wit enough to recognize him.Cleon rushes out of the house. Oh! mercy! here comes the Paphlagonian!

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: By the twelve gods! Woe betide you, who have too long been conspiring against Demos. What means this Chalcidian cup? No doubt you are provoking the Chalcidians to revolt. You shall be killed and butchered, you brace of rogues.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: What! are you for running away? Come, come, stand firm, bold Sausage-seller, do not betray us.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: To the rescue, oh, Knights. Now is the time. Simon, Panaetius, get you to the right wing; they are coming on; hold tight and return to the charge. I can see the dust of their horses' hoofs; they are galloping to our aid. Courage! Attack him, put him to flight.

div.stage: The Chorus of Knights enters at top speed.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Strike, strike the villain, who has spread confusion amongst the ranks of the Knights, this public robber, this yawning gulf of plunder, this devouring Charybdis, this villain, this villain, this villain! I cannot say the word too often, for he is a villain a thousand times a day. Come, strike, drive, hurl him over and crush him to pieces; hate him as we hate him; stun him with your blows and your shouts. And beware lest he escape you; he knows the way Eucrates took straight to a bran sack for concealment.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Oh! veteran Heliasts, brotherhood of the three obols, whom I fostered by bawling at random, help me; I am being beaten to death by rebels.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: And justly too; you devour the public funds that all should share in; you treat the treasury officials like the fruit of the fig tree, squeezing them to find which are still green or more or less ripe; and, when you find a simple and timid one, you force him to come from the Chersonese, then you seize him by the middle, throttle him by the neck, while you twist his shoulder back; he falls and you devour him. Besides, you know very well how to select from among the citizens those who are as meek as lambs, rich, without guile and loathers of lawsuits.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Eh! what! Knights, are you helping them? But, if I am beaten, it is in your cause, for I was going to propose to erect a statue in the city in memory of your bravery.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Oh! the impostor! the dull varlet! See! he treats us like old dotards and crawls at our feet to deceive us; but the cunning wherein his power lies shall this time recoil on himself; he trips up himself by resorting to such artifices.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Oh citizens! oh people! see how these brutes are bursting my belly.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: What shouts! but it's this very bawling that incessantly upsets the city!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I can shout too—and so loud that you will flee with fear.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: If you shout louder than he does I will strike up the triumphal hymn; if you surpass him in impudence the cake is ours.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I denounce this fellow; he has had tasty stews exported from Athens for the Spartan fleet.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And I denounce him; he runs into the Prytaneum with an empty belly and comes out with it full.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: And by Zeus! he carries off bread, meat, and fish, which is forbidden. Pericles himself never had this right.

div.stage: A screaming match now ensues, each line more raucous than the last. The rapidity of the dialogue likewise increases.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: You are travelling the right road to get killed.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I'll bawl three times as loud as you.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I will deafen you with my yells.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And I you with my bellowing.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I shall calumniate you, if you become a Strategus.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Dog, I will lay your back open with the lash.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I will make you drop your arrogance.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I will baffle your machinations.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Dare to look me in the face!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I too was brought up in the market-place.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I will cut you to shreds if you whisper a word.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: If you open your mouth, I'll shut it with shit.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I admit I'm a thief; that's more than you do.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: By our Hermes of the market-place, if caught in the act, why, I perjure myself before those who saw me.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: These are my own special tricks. I will denounce you to the Prytanes as the owner of sacred tripe, that has not paid tithe.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Oh! you scoundrel! you impudent bawler! everything is filled with your daring, all Attica, the Assembly, the Treasury, the decrees, the tribunals. As a furious torrent you have overthrown our city; your outcries have deafened Athens and, posted upon a high rock, you have lain in wait for the tribute moneys as the fisherman does for the tunny-fish.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I know your tricks; it's an old plot resoled.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: If you know naught of soling, I understand nothing of sausages; you, who cut bad leather on the slant to make it look stout and deceive the country yokels. They had not worn it a day before it had stretched some two spans.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: That's the very trick he played on me; both my neighbors and my friends laughed heartily at me, and before I reached Pergasae I was swimming in my shoes.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Have you not always shown that blatant impudence, which is the sole strength of our orators? You push it so far, that you, the head of the State, dare to milk the purses of the opulent aliens and, at sight of you, the son of Hippodamus melts into tears. But here is another man who gives me pleasure, for he is a much greater rascal than you; he will overthrow you; 'tis easy to see, that he will beat you in roguery, in brazenness and in clever turns.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Come, you, who have been brought up among the class which to-day gives us all our great men, show us that a liberal education is mere tomfoolery.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Yes, hear what sort of citizen he is.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Won't you let me speak?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Assuredly not, for I too am an awful rascal.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: If he does not give in at that, tell him your parents were awful rascals too.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Once more, will you let me speak?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: No, by Zeus!

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Yes, by Zeus, you shall!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: No, by Poseidon! We will fight first to see who shall speak first.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I will die sooner.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I will not let you .

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Let him, in the name of the gods, let him die.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: What makes you so bold as to dare to speak to my face?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Because I know both how to speak and how to cook.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Hah! the fine speaker! Truly, if some business matter fell your way,you would know thoroughly well how to attack it, to carve it up alive! Shall I tell you what has happened to you? Like so many others, you have gained some petty lawsuit against some alien. Did you drink enough water to inspire you? Did you mutter over the thing sufficiently through the night, spout it along the street, recite it to all you met? Have you bored your friends enough with it? And for this you deem yourself an orator. You poor fool!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And what do you drink yourself then, to be able all alone by yourself to dumbfound and stupefy the city so with your clamor?

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Can you match me with a rival? Me? When I have devoured a good hot tunny-fish and drunk on top of it a great jar of unmixed wine. I say “to Hell with the generals of Pylos!”

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And I, when I have bolted the tripe of an ox together with a sow's belly and swallowed the broth as well, I am fit, though slobbering with grease, to bellow louder than all orators and to terrify Nicias.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: I admire your language so much; the only thing I do not approve is that you swallow all the broth yourself.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Even though you gorged yourself on sea-dogs, you would not beat the Milesians.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Give me a bullock's breast to devour, and I am a man to traffic in mines.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I will rush into the Senate and set them all by the ears.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And I will pull out your arse to stuff like a sausage.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: As for me, I will seize you by the rump and hurl your head foremost through the door.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: By Poseidon, only after you have thrown me there first.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.stage: Beginning another crescendo of competitive screeching
sp.p: Beware of the carcan!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I denounce you for cowardice.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I will tan your hide.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I will flay you and make a thief's pouch with the skin.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I will peg you out on the ground.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I will slice you into mince-meat.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I will tear out your eyelashes.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I will slit your gullet.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: We will set his mouth open with a wooden stick as the cooks do with pigs; we will tear out his tongue, and, looking down his gaping throat, will see whether his inside has any pimples.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Thus then at Athens we have something more fiery than fire, more impudent than impudence itself! 'Tis a grave matter; come, we will push and jostle him without mercy. There, you grip him tightly under the arms; if he gives way at the onset, you will find him nothing but a craven; I know my man.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: That he has been all his life and he has only made himself a name by reaping another's harvest; and now he has tied up the ears he gathered over there, he lets them dry and seeks to sell them.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I do not fear you as long as there is a Senate and a people which stands like a fool, gaping in the air.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: What unparalleled impudence! 'Tis ever the same brazen front. If I don't hate you, why, I'm ready to take the place of the one blanket Cratinus wets; I'll offer to play a tragedy by Morsimus. Oh! you cheat! who turn all into money, who flutter from one extortion to another; may you disgorge as quickly as you have crammed yourself! Then only would I sing, “Let us drink, let us drink to this happy event!”
Then even the son of Ulius, the old wheat-fairy, would empty his cup with transports of joy, crying, “Io, Paean! Io, Bacchus!”

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: By Poseidon! You! would you beat me in impudence! If you succeed, may I no longer have my share of the victims offered to Zeus on the city altar.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And I, I swear by the blows that have so oft rained upon my shoulders since infancy, and by the knives that have cut me, that I will show more effrontery than you; as sure as I have rounded this fine stomach by feeding on the pieces of bread that had cleansed other folk's greasy fingers.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: On pieces of bread, like a dog! Ah! wretch! you have the nature of a dog and you dare to fight a dog-headed ape?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I have many another trick in my sack, memories of my childhood's days. I used to linger around the cooks and say to them, “Look, friends don't you see a swallow? It's the herald of springtime.” And while they stood, their noses in the air, I made off with a piece of meat.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Oh! most clever man! How well thought out! You did as the eaters of artichokes, you gathered them before the return of the swallows.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: They could make nothing of it; or, if they suspected a trick, I hid the meat in my crotch and denied the thing by all the gods; so that an orator, seeing me at the game, cried, “This child will get on; he has the mettle that makes a statesman.”

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: He argued rightly; to steal, perjure yourself and make your arse receptive are three essentials for climbing high.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I will stop your insolence, or rather the insolence of both of you. I will throw myself upon you like a terrible hurricane ravaging both land and sea at the will of its fury.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Then I will gather up my sausages and entrust myself to the kindly waves of fortune so as to make you all the more enraged.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: And I will watch in the bilges in case the boat should make water.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: No, by Demeter! I swear, it will not be with impunity that you have thieved so many talents from the Athenians.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Oh! oh! reef your sail a bit! Here is a Northeaster blowing calumniously.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I know that you got ten talents out of Potidaea.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Wait! I will give you one; but keep it dark!

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Hah! that will please him mightily;

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Now you can travel under full sail. The wind has lost its violence.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I will bring four suits against you, each of one hundred talents.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And I twenty against you for shirking duty and more than a thousand for robbery.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I maintain that your parents were guilty of sacrilege against the goddess.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And I, that one of your grandfathers was a satellite....

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: To whom? Explain!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: To Byrsina, the mother of Hippias.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: You are an impostor.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And you are a rogue.
sp.stage: He strikes Cleon with a sausage.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Hit him hard.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Alas! The conspirators are murdering me!

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Hit him! Hit him with all your might! Bruise his belly and lash him with your guts and your tripe! Punish him with both hands!Cleon sinks beneath the blows.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Oh! vigorous assailant and intrepid heart! See how you have totally routed him in this duel of abuse, so that to us and to the citizens you seem the saviour of the city. How shall I give tongue to my joy and praise you sufficiently?

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Ah! by Demeter! I was not ignorant of this plot and these machinations that were being forged and nailed and put together against me.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Look out, look out! Come, outfence him with some wheelwright slang.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: His tricks at Argos do not escape me. Under pretence of forming an alliance with the Argives, he is hatching a plot with the Lacedaemonians there; and I know why the bellows are blowing and the metal that is on the anvil; it's the question of the prisoners.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Well done! Forge on, if he be a wheelwright.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And there are men at Sparta who are hammering the iron with you; but neither gold nor silver nor prayers nor anything else shall impede my denouncing your trickery to the Athenians.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: As for me, I hasten to the Senate to reveal your plotting, your nightly gatherings in the city, your trafficking with the Medes and with the Great King, and all you are foraging for in Boeotia.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: What price then is paid for forage by Boeotians?

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Oh! by Heracles! I will tan your hide.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Come, if you have both wit and heart, now is the time to show it, as on the day when you hid the meat in your crotch, as you say. Hasten to the Senate, for he will rush there like a tornado to calumniate us all and give vent to his fearful bellowings.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I am going, but first I must rid myself of my tripe and my knives; I will leave them here.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Stay! rub your neck with lard; in this way you will slip between the fingers of calumny.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Spoken like a finished wrestling coach.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Now, bolt down these cloves of garlic.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Pray, what for?

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: Well primed with garlic, you will have greater mettle for the fight. But hurry, make haste rapidly!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: That's just what I'm doing.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: And, above all, bite your foe, rend him to atoms, tear off his comb and do not return until you have devoured his wattles. He goes into the house of Demos.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Go! make your attack with a light heart, avenge me and may Zeus guard you! I burn to see you return the victor and laden with chaplets of glory. And you, spectators, enlightened critics of all kind of poetry, lend an ear to my anapests.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.stage: The Chorus moves forward and faces the audience.
sp.p: Had one of the old authors asked me to mount this stage to recite his verses, he would not have found it hard to persuade me. But our poet of to-day is likewise worthy of this favour; he shares our hatred, he dares to tell the truth, he boldly braves both waterspouts and hurricanes. Many among you, he tells us, have expressed wonder, that he has not long since had a piece presented in his own name, and have asked the reason why. This is what he bids us say in reply to your questions; it is not without grounds that he has courted the shade, for, in his opinion, nothing is more difficult than to cultivate the comic Muse; many court her, but very few secure her favours. Moreover, he knows that you are fickle by nature and betray your poets when they grow old. What fate befell Magnes, when his hair went white? Often enough had he triumphed over his rivals; he had sung in all keys, played the lyre and fluttered wings; he turned into a Lydian and even into a gnat, daubed himself with green to become a frog. All in vain! When young, you applauded him; in his old age you hooted and mocked him, because his genius for raillery had gone. Cratinus again was like a torrent of glory rushing across the plain, up-rooting oak, plane tree and rivals and bearing them pell-mell in his wake. The only songs at the banquet were, “Doro, shod with lying tales” and “Adepts of the Lyric Muse,” so great was his renown. Look at him now! he drivels, his lyre has neither strings nor keys, his voice quivers, but you have no pity for him, and you let him wander about as he can, like Connas, his temples circled with a withered chaplet; the poor old fellow is dying of thirst; he who, in honor of his glorious past, should be in the Prytaneum drinking at his ease, and instead of trudging the country should be sitting amongst the first row of the spectators, close to the statue of Dionysus and loaded with perfumes. Crates, again, have you done hounding him with your rage and your hisses? True, it was but meagre fare that his sterile Muse could offer you; a few ingenious fancies formed the sole ingredients, but nevertheless he knew how to stand firm and to recover from his falls It is such examples that frighten our poet; in addition, he would tell himself, that before being a pilot, he must first know how to row, then to keep watch at the prow, after that how to gauge the winds, and that only then would he be able to command his vessel. If then you approve this wise caution and his resolve that he would not bore you with foolish nonsense,

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: raise loud waves of applause in his favour this day, so that, at this Lenaean feast, the breath of your favour may swell the sails of his triumphant galley and the poet may withdraw proud of his success, with head erect and his face beaming with delight.

sp.speaker: First Semi-Chorus
sp.p: Poseidon, god of the racing steeds, I salute you, you who delight in their neighing and in the resounding clatter of their brass-shod hoofs, god of the swift galleys, which, loaded with mercenaries, cleave the seas with their azure beaks, god of the equestrian contests, in which young rivals, eager for glory, ruin themselves for the sake of distinction with their chariots in the arena, come and direct our chorus; Poseidon with the trident of gold, you, who reign over the dolphins, who are worshipped at Sunium and at Geraestus beloved of Phormio, and dear to the whole city above all the immortals, I salute you!

sp.speaker: Leader of First Semi-Chorus
sp.p: Let us sing the glory of our forefathers; ever victors, both on land and sea, they merit that Athens, rendered famous by these, her worthy sons, should write their deeds upon the sacred peplus. As soon as they saw the enemy, they at once sprang at him without ever counting his strength. Should one of them fall in the conflict he would shake off the dust, deny his mishap and begin the struggle anew. Not one of these generals of old time would have asked Cleaenetus to be fed at the cost of the State; but our present men refuse to fight, unless they get the honors of the Prytaneum and precedence in their seats. As for us, we place our valor gratuitously at the service of Athens and of her gods; our only hope is that, should peace ever put a term to our toils, you will not grudge us our long, scented hair nor our delicate care for our toilet.

sp.speaker: Second Semi-Chorus
sp.p: Oh! Pallas, guardian of Athens, you, who reign over the most pious city, the most powerful, the richest in warriors and in poets, hasten to my call, bringing in your train our faithful ally in all our expeditions and combats, Victory, who smiles on our choruses and fights with us against our rivals. Oh! goddess! manifest yourself to our sight; this day more than ever we deserve that you should ensure our triumph.

sp.speaker: Leader of Second Semi-Chorus
sp.p: We will sing likewise the exploits of our steeds! they are worthy of our praises; in what invasions, what fights have I not seen them helping us! But especially admirable were they, when they bravely leapt upon the galleys, taking nothing with them but a coarse wine, some cloves of garlic and onions; despite this, they nevertheless seized the sweeps just like men, curved their backs over the thwarts and shouted, “Hippapai! Give way! Come, all pull together! Come, come! How! Samphoras! Are you not rowing?” They rushed down upon the coast of Corinth, and the youngesthollowed out beds in the sand with their hoofs or went to fetch coverings; instead of luzern, they had no food but crabs, which they caught on the strand and even in the sea; so that Theorus causes a Corinthian crab to say, “'Tis a cruel fate, oh Poseidon neither my deep hiding-places, whether on land or at sea, can help me to escape the Knights.”

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Welcome, oh, dearest and bravest of men! How distracted I have been during your absence! But here you are back, safe and sound. Tell us about the fight you have had.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: The important thing is that I have beaten the Senate.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: All glory to you! Let us burst into shouts of joy! You speak well, but your deeds are even better. Come, tell me everything in detail; what a long journey would I not be ready to take to hear your tale! Come, dear friend, speak with full confidence to your admirers.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: The story is worth hearing. Listen! From here I rushed straight to the Senate, right in the track of this man; he was already letting loose the storm, unchaining the lightning, crushing the Knights beneath huge mountains of calumnies heaped together and having all the air of truth; he called you conspirators and his lies caught root like weeds in every mind; dark were the looks on every side and brows were knitted. When I saw that the Senate listened to him favorably and was being tricked by his imposture I said to myself, “Come, gods of rascals and braggarts, gods of all fools, and toad-eaters, and thou too, oh market-place, wherein I was bred from my earliest days, give me unbridled audacity, an untiring chatter and a shameless voice.” No sooner had I ended this prayer than a pederast farted on my right. “Hah! a good omen,” said I, and prostrated myself; then I burst open the door by a vigorous push with my arse, and, opening my mouth to the utmost, shouted, “Senators, I wanted you to be the first to hear the good news; since the war broke out, I have never seen anchovies at a lower price!” All faces brightened at once and I was voted a chaplet for my good tidings; and I added, “With a couple of words I will reveal to you how you can have quantities of anchovies for an obol; all you have to do is to seize on all the dishes the merchants have.” With mouths gaping with admiration, they applauded me. However, the Paphlagonian winded the matter and, well knowing the sort of language which pleases the Senate best, said, “Friends, I am resolved to offer one hundred oxen to the goddess in recognition of this happy event.” The Senate at once veered to his side.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: So when I saw myself defeated by this ox dung, I outbade the fellow, crying, “Two hundred!” And beyond this I moved that a vow be made to Diana of a thousand goats if the next day anchovies should only be worth an obol a hundred. And the Senate looked towards me again. The other, stunned with the blow, grew delirious in his speech, and at last the Prytanes and the Scythians dragged him out. The Senators then stood talking noisily about the anchovies. Cleon, however, begged them to listen to the Lacedaemonian envoy, who had come to make proposals of peace; but all with one accord cried “Certainly it's not the moment to think of peace now! If anchovies are so cheap, what need have we of peace? Let the war take its course!” And with loud shouts they demanded that the Prytanes should close the sitting and then they leapt over the rails in all directions. As for me, I slipped away to buy all the coriander seed and leeks there were on the market and gave it to them gratis as seasoning for their anchovies. It was marvellous! They loaded me with praises and caresses; thus I conquered the Senate with an obol's worth of leeks, and here I am.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Bravo! you are the spoilt child of Fortune. Ah! our knave has found his match in another, who has far better tricks in his sack, a thousand kinds of knaveries and of wily words. But the fight begins afresh; take care not to weaken; you know that I have long been your most faithful ally.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Ah! ah! here comes the Paphlagonian! One would say it was a hurricane lashing the sea and rolling the waves before it in its fury. He looks as if he wanted to swallow me up alive! Ye gods! what an impudent knave!

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: To my aid, my beloved lies! I am going to destroy you, or my name is lost.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Oh! how he diverts me with his threats! His bluster makes me laugh! And I dance the mothon for joy, and sing at the top of my voice, cuckoo!

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Ah! by Demeter! if I do not kill and devour you, may I die!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: If you do not devour me? and I, if I do not drink your blood to the last drop, and then burst with indigestion.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I, I will strangle you, I swear it by the front seat which Pylos gained me.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: By the front seat! Ah! might I see you fall into the hindmost seat!

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: By heaven! I will put you to the torture.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: What a lively wit! Come, what's the best to give you to eat? What do you prefer? A purse?

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I will tear out your insides with my nails.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And I will cut off your victuals at the Prytaneum.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I will haul you before Demos, who will mete out justice to you.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And I too will drag you before him and belch forth more calumnies than you.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Why, poor fool, he does not believe you, whereas I play with him at will.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Is then Demos your property, your contemptible creature?

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: It's because I know the dishes that please him.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And these are little mouthfuls, which you serve to him like a clever nurse. You chew the pieces and place some in small quantities in his mouth, while you swallow three parts yourself.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Thanks to my skill, I know exactly how to enlarge or contract this gullet.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: My arse is just as clever.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Well, my friend, you tricked me at the Senate, but take care! Let us go before Demos.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: That's easily done; come, let's do it right away.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Oh, Demos! Come out here.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: By Zeus, Father, come on out!

sp.speaker: Kleon
sp.p: Come, oh, my dear little Demos; come and see how I am insulted.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.stage: Coming out of his house followed by Demosthenes
sp.p: What a hubhub! To the Devil with you, bawlers! Alas! my olive branch, which they have torn down! Ah! it's you, Paphlagonian. And who, pray, has been maltreating you?

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: You are the cause of this man and these young people having covered me with blows.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: And why?

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Because you love me passionately, Demos.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: And you, who are you?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: His rival. For many a long year have I loved you, have I wished to do you honor, I and a crowd of other men of means. But this rascal here has prevented us. You resemble those young men who do not know where to choose their lovers; you repulse honest folks; to earn your favours, one has to be a lamp-seller, a cobbler, a tanner or a currier.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I am the benefactor of the people.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: In what way, please?

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: In what way? I supplanted the Generals at Pylos, I hurried thither and I brought back the Laconian captives.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And I, whilst simply loitering, cleared off with a pot from a shop, which another fellow had been boiling.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Demos, convene the assembly at once to decide which of us two loves you best and most merits your favour.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Yes, yes, provided it be not at the Pnyx.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: I could not sit elsewhere; it is at the Pnyx that you must appear before me.

div.stage: He sits down on a stone in the Orchestra.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Ah! great gods! I am undone! At home this old fellow is the most sensible of men, but the instant he is seated on those cursed stone seats, he is there with mouth agape as if he were hanging up figs by their stems to dry.

sp.speaker: First Semi-Chorus
sp.p: Come, loose all sail. Be bold, skilful in attack and entangle him in arguments which admit of no reply. It is difficult to beat him, for he is full of craft and pulls himself out of the worst corners. Collect all your forces to come forth from this fight covered with glory.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: But take care! Let him not assume the attack, get ready your grapples and advance with your vessel to board him!

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Oh! guardian goddess of our city! oh! Athena if it be true that next to Lysicles, Cynna and Salabaccho none have done so much good for the Athenian people as I, suffer me to continue to be fed at the Prytaneum without working; but if I hate you, if I am not ready to fight in your defence alone and against all, may I perish, be sawn to bits alive and my skin cut up into thongs.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And I, Demos, if it be not true, that I love and cherish you, may I be cooked in a stew; and if that is not saying enough, may I be grated on this table with some cheese and then hashed, may a hook be passed through my balls and let me be dragged thus to the Ceramicus!

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Is it possible, Demos, to love you more than I do? And firstly, as long as you have governed with my consent, have I not filled your treasury, putting pressure on some, torturing others or begging of them, indifferent to the opinion of private individuals, and solely anxious to please you?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: There is nothing so wonderful in all that, Demos; I will do as much; I will thieve the bread of others to serve up to you. No, he has neither love for you nor kindly feeling; his only care is to warm himself with your wood, and I will prove it. You, who, sword in hand, saved Attica from the Median yoke at Marathon; you, whose glorious triumphs we love to extol unceasingly, look, he cares little whether he sees you seated uncomfortably upon a stone; whereas I, I bring you this cushion, which I have sewn with my own hands. Rise and try this nice soft seat. Did you not put enough strain on your bottom at Salamis?
sp.stage: He gives Demos the cushion; Demos sits on it.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Who are you then? Can you be of the race of Harmodius? Upon my faith, that is nobly done and like a true friend of Demos.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Petty flattery to prove him your goodwill!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: But you have caught him with even smaller baits!

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: > Never had Demos a defender or a friend more devoted than myself; on my head, on my life, I swear it!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: You pretend to love him and for eight years you have seen him housed in casks, in crevices and dovecots, where he is blinded with the smoke, and you lock him in without pity; Archeptolemus brought peace and you tore it to ribbons; the envoys who come to propose a truce you drive from the city with kicks in their arses.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: The purpose of this is that Demos may rule over all the Greeks; for the oracles predict that, if he is patient, he must one day sit as judge in Arcadia at five obols per day. Meanwhile, I will nourish him, look after him and, above all, I will ensure to him his three obols.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: No, little you care for his reigning in Arcadia, it's to pillage and impose on the allies at will that you reckon; you wish the war to conceal your rogueries as in a mist, that Demos may see nothing of them, and harassed by cares, may only depend on yourself for his bread. But if ever peace is restored to him, if ever he returns to his lands to comfort himself once more with good cakes, to greet his cherished olives, he will know the blessings you have kept him out of, even though paying him a salary; and, filled with hatred and rage, he will rise, burning with desire to vote against you. You know this only too well; it is for this you rock him to sleep with your lies.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Is it not shameful, that you should dare thus to calumniate me before Demos, me, to whom Athens, I swear it by Demeter, already owes more than it ever did to Themistocles?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Oh! citizens of Argos, do you hear what he says?

You dare to compare yourself to Themistocles, who found our city half empty and left it full to overflowing, who one day gave us the Piraeus for dinner, and added fresh fish to all our usual meals. You, on the contrary, you, who compare yourself with Themistocles, have only sought to reduce our city in size, to shut it within its walls, to chant oracles to us. And Themistocles goes into exile, while you gorge yourself on the most excellent fare

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Oh! Demos! Am I compelled to hear myself thus abused, and merely because I love you?

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Silence! stop your abuse! All too long have I been your dupe.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Ah! my dear little Demos, he is a rogue who has played you many a scurvy trick;

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: when your back is turned, he taps at the root the lawsuits initiated by the peculators, swallows the proceeds wholesale and helps himself with both hands from the public funds.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Tremble, knave; I will convict you of having stolen thirty thousand drachmae.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: For a rascal of your kidney, you shout rarely! Well! I am ready to die if I do not prove that you have accepted more than forty minae from the Mitylenaeans.

sp.speaker: Second Semi-Chorus
sp.p: This indeed may be termed talking. Oh, benefactor of the human race, proceed and you will be the most illustrious of the Greeks. You alone shall have sway in Athens, the allies will obey you, and, trident in hand, you will go about shaking and overturning everything to enrich yourself.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: But, stick to your man, let him not go; with lungs like yours you will soon have him finished.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: No, my brave friends, no, you are running too fast; I have done a sufficiently brilliant deed to shut the mouth of all enemies, so long as one of the bucklers of Pylos remains.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Of the bucklers! Hold! I stop you there and I hold you fast. For if it be true that you love the people, you would not allow these to be hung up with their rings; but it's with an intent you have done this. Demos, take knowledge of his guilty purpose; in this way you no longer can punish him at your pleasure. Note the swarm of young tanners, who really surround him, and close to them the sellers of honey and cheese; all these are at one with him. Very well! you have but to frown, to speak of ostracism and they will rush at night to these bucklers, take them down and seize our granaries.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Great gods! what! the bucklers retain their rings! Scoundrel! ah! too long have you had me for your dupe, cheated and played with me!

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: But, dear sir, never you believe all he tells you. Oh! never will you find a more devoted friend than me; unaided, I have known how to put down the conspiracies; nothing that is hatching in the city escapes me, and I hasten to proclaim it loudly.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: You are like the fishers for eels; in still waters they catch nothing, but if they thoroughly stir up the slime, their fishing is good; in the same way it's only in troublous times that you line your pockets. But come, tell me, you, who sell so many skins, have you ever made him a present of a pair of soles for his slippers? and you pretend to love him!

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: No, he has never given me any.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: That alone shows up the man; but I, I have bought you this pair of shoes; accept them.
sp.stage: He gives Demos the shoes; Demos puts them on.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: None ever, to my knowledge, has merited so much from the people; you are the most zealous of all men for your country and for my toes.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Can a wretched pair of slippers make you forget all that you owe me? Is it not I who curbed the pederasts by erasing Gryttus' name from the lists of citizens?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Ah! noble Inspector of Arses, let me congratulate you. Moreover, if you set yourself against this form of lewdness, this pederasty, it was for sheer jealousy, knowing it to be the school for orators. But you see this poor Demos without a cloak and that at his age too! so little do you care for him, that in mid-winter you have not given him a garment with sleeves. Here, Demos, here is one, take it!
sp.stage: He gives Demos a cloak; Demos puts it on.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: This even Themistocles never thought of; the Piraeus was no doubt a happy idea, but I think this tunic is quite as fine as invention.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Must you have recourse to such jackanapes' tricks to supplant me?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: No, it's your own tricks that I am borrowing, just as a drunken guest, when he has to take a crap, seizes some other man's shoes.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Oh! you shall not outdo me in flattery! I am going to hand Demos this garment; all that remains to you, you rogue, is to go and hang yourself.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.stage: as Cleon throws a cloak around his shoulders
sp.p: Faugh! may the plague seize you! You stink of leather horribly.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Why, it's to smother you that he has thrown this cloak around you on top of the other; and it is not the first plot he has planned against you. Do you remember the time when silphium was so cheap?

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Aye, to be sure I do!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Very well! it was Cleon who had caused the price to fall so low, that all might eat it, and the jurymen in the Courts were almost asphyxiated from farting in each others' faces.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Hah! why, indeed, a Dungtownite told me the same thing.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Were you not yourself in those days quite red in the gills with farting?

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Why, it was a trick worthy of Pyrrhandrus!

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: With what other idle trash will you seek to ruin me, you wretch!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Oh! I shall be more brazen than you, for it's the goddess who has commanded me.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: No, on my honor, you will not! Here, Demos, feast on this dish; it is your salary as a dicast, which you gain through me for doing naught.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Wait! here is a little box of ointment to rub into the sores on your legs.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I will pluck out your white hairs and make you young again.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Take this hare's tail to wipe the rheum from your eyes.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: When you wipe your nose, clean your fingers on my head.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: No, on mine.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: On mine. I will have you made a trierarch and you will get ruined through it; I will arrange that you are given an old vessel with rotten sails, which you will have to repair constantly and at great cost.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Our man is on the boil; enough, enough, he is boiling over; remove some of the embers from under him and skim off his threats.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I will punish your self-importance; I will crush you with imposts; I will have you inscribed on the list of the rich.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Splendid! by Zeus, Apollo and Demeter!

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Faith! here is an excellent citizen indeed, such as has not been seen for a long time. He's truly a man of the lowest scum! As for you, Paphlagonian, who pretend to love me, you only feed me on garlic. Return me my ring, for you cease to be my steward.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Here it is, but be assured, that if you bereave me of my power, my successor will be worse than I am.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: This cannot be my ring; I see another device, unless I am going purblind.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: What was your device?

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: A fig-leaf, stuffed with bullock's fat.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: No, that is not it.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: What is it then?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: It's a gull with beak wide open, haranguing the people from the top of a stone.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Ah! great gods!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: What is the matter?

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Away! away out of my sight! It's not my ring he had, it was that of Cleonymus. To the Sausage-Seller Wait, I'll give you this one; you shall be my steward.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Master, I adjure you, decide nothing till you have heard my oracles.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And mine.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: If you believe him, you will have to prostitute yourself for him.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: If you listen to him, you'll have to let him peel you to the very stump.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: My oracles say that you are to reign over the whole earth, crowned with chaplets.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And mine say that, clothed in an embroidered purple robe, you shall pursue Smicythe and her spouse, standing in a chariot of gold and with a crown on your head.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Go, fetch me your oracles, that the Paphlagonian may hear them.

sp.speaker: Demosthenes
sp.p: By all means. And you fetch yours.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Here goes.
sp.stage: He rushes into the house of Demos.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Here goes, by Zeus! There's nothing to stop us.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Oh! happy day for us and for our children if Cleon perish. Yet just now I heard some old cross-grained pleaders on the market-place who hold not this opinion discoursing together. Said they, “If Cleon had not had the power, we should have lacked two most useful tools, the pestle and the soup-ladle.”

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: You also know what a pig's education he has had; his school-fellows can recall that he only liked the Dorian style and would study no other; his music-master in displeasure sent him away, saying; “This youth, in matters of harmony, will only learn the Dorian style because it is akin to bribery.”

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.stage: coming out of the house with a large package
sp.p: There, look at this heap; and yet I'm not bringing them all.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.stage: entering with an even larger package
sp.p: Ugh! The weight of them is squeezing the crap right out of me, and still I'm not bringing them all!

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: What are these?

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Oracles.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: All these?

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Does that astonish you? Why, I have another whole boxful of them.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And I the whole of my attic and two rooms besides.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Come, let us see, whose are these oracles?

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Mine are those of Bacis.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: And whose are yours?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Glanis's, the elder brother of Bacis.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: And of what do they speak?

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Of Athens and Pylos and you and me and everything.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: And yours?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Of Athens and lentils and Lacedaemonians and fresh mackerel and scoundrelly flour-sellers and you and me. Ah! ha! now watch him gnaw his own tool with chagrin!

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Come, read them out to me and especially that one I like so much, which says that I shall become an eagle and soar among the clouds.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Then listen and be attentive!

“Son of Erechtheus, understand the meaning of the words, which the sacred tripods set resounding in the sanctuary of Apollo. Preserve the sacred dog with the jagged teeth, that barks and howls in your defence; he will ensure you a salary and, if he fails, will perish as the victim of the swarms of jays that hunt him down with their screams.”

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: By Demeter! I do not understand a word of it. What connection is there between Erechtheus, the jays and the dog?

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I am the dog, since I bark in your defence. Well! Phoebus commands you to keep and cherish your dog.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: That is not what the god says; this dog seems to me to gnaw at the oracles as others gnaw at doorposts. Here is exactly what Apollo says of the dog.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Let us hear, but I must first pick up a stone; an oracle which speaks of a dog might bite my tool.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: “Son of Erechtheus, beware of this Cerberus that enslaves free men; he fawns upon you with his tail when you are dining, but he is lying in wait to devour your dishes should you turn your head an instant; at night he sneaks into the kitchen and, true dog that he is, licks up with one lap of his tongue both your dishes and ... the islands.”

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: By god, Glanis, you speak better than your brother.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Condescend again to hear me and then judge:

“A woman in sacred Athens will be delivered of a lion, who shall fight for the people against clouds of gnats with the same ferocity as if he were defending his whelps; care ye for him, erect wooden walls around him and towers of brass.”
Do you understand that?

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Not the least bit in the world.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: The god tells you here to look after me, for I am your lion.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: How! You have become a lion and I never knew a thing about it?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: There is only one thing which he purposely keeps from you; he does not say what this wall of wood and brass is in which Apollo warns you to keep and guard him.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: What does the god mean, then?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: He advises you to fit him into a five-holed wooden collar.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Hah! I think that oracle is about to be fulfilled.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Do not believe it; these are but jealous crows, that caw against me; but never cease to cherish your good hawk; never forget that he brought you those Lacedaemonian fish, loaded with chains.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Ah! if the Paphlagonian ran any risk that day, it was because he was drunk. Oh, too credulous son of Cecrops, do you accept that as a glorious exploit? A woman would carry a heavy burden if only a man had put it on her shoulders. But to fight! Go to! he would empty his bowels before he would ever fight.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Note this Pylos in front of Pylos, of which the oracle speaks, “Pylos is before Pylos.”

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: How “in front of Pylos”? What does he mean by that?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: He says he will seize upon your bath-tubs.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Then I shall not bathe to-day.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: No, as he has stolen our baths. But here is an oracle about the fleet, to which I beg your best attention.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Read on! I am listening; let us first see how we are to pay our sailors.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: “Son of Aegeus, beware of the tricks of the dog-fox, he bites from the rear and rushes off at full speed; he is nothing but cunning and perfidy.” Do you know what the oracle intends to say?

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: The dog-fox is Philostratus.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: No, no, it's Cleon; he is incessantly asking you for light vessels to go and collect the tributes, and Apollo advises you not to grant them.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: What connection is there between a galley and dog-fox?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: What connection? Why, it's quite plain —a galley travels as fast as a dog.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Why, then, does the oracle not say dog instead of dog-fox?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Because he compares the soldiers to young foxes, who, like them, eat the grapes in the fields.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Good! Well then! how am I to pay the wages of my young foxes?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I will undertake that, and in three days too! But listen to this further oracle, by which Apollo puts you on your guard against the snares of the greedy fist.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Of what greedy fist?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: The god in this oracle very clearly points to the hand of Cleon, who incessantly holds his out, saying, “Fill it.”

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: That's a lie! Phoebus means the hand of Diopeithes. But here I have a winged oracle, which promises you shall become an eagle and rule over all the earth.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I have one, which says that you shall be King of the Earth and of the Red Sea too, and that you shall administer justice in Ecbatana, eating fine rich stews the while.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I have seen Athena in a dream, pouring out full vials of riches and health over the people.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I too have seen the goddess, descending from the Acropolis with an owl perched upon her helmet; on your head she was pouring out ambrosia, on that of Cleon garlic pickle.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Truly Glanis is the wisest of men. I shall yield myself to you; guide me in my old age and educate me anew.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Ah! I adjure you! not yet; wait a little; I will promise to distribute barley every day.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Ah! I will not hear another word about barley; you have cheated me too often already, both you and Theophanes.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Well then! you shall have flour-cakes all piping hot.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I will give you cakes too, and nice cooked fish; all you'll have to do is eat.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Very well, mind you keep your promises. To whichever of you shall treat me best I hand over the reins of state.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I will be first.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: No, no, I will.He runs off.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Demos, you are our all-powerful sovereign lord; all tremble before you, yet you are led by the nose. You love to be flattered and fooled; you listen to the orators with gaping mouth and your mind is led astray.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: It's rather you who have no brains, if you think me so foolish as all that; it is with a purpose that I play this idiot's role, for I love to drink the livelong day, and so it pleases me to keep a thief for my minister. When he has thoroughly gorged himself, then I overthrow and crush him.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: What profound wisdom! If it be really so, why! all is for the best. Your ministers, then, are your victims, whom you nourish and feed up expressly in the Pnyx, so that, the day your dinner is ready, you may immolate the fattest and eat him.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Look, see how I play with them, while all the time they think themselves such adepts at cheating me. I have my eye on them when they thieve, but I do not appear to be seeing them; then I thrust a judgment down their throat as it were a feather, and force them to vomit up all they have robbed from me.

sp.stage: Cleon comes out of the house with a bench and a large basket; at the same moment the Sausage-Seller arrives with another basket; the two are placed beside one another.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Get out of here!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Get out yourself!

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Demos, all is ready these three hours; I await your orders and I burn with desire to load you with benefits.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And I ten, twelve, a thousand hours, a long, long while, an infinitely long, long, long while.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: As for me, it's thirty thousand hours that I have been impatient; very long, infinitely long, long, long that I have cursed you.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Do you know what you had best do?

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: I will, if you tell me.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Declare the lists open and we will contend abreast to determine who shall treat you the best.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Splendid! Draw back in line!

sp.speaker: Cleon and Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Ready.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Off you go!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I shall not let you get to the tape.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: What fervent lovers! If I am not to-day the happiest of men, it will be because I am the most disgusted.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.stage: Putting down the bench for Demos
sp.p: Look! I am the first to bring you a seat.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And I a table.

div.stage: He places his sausage-tray in front of Demos

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Wait, here is a cake kneaded of Pylos barley.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Here are crusts, which the ivory hand of the goddess has hallowed.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Oh! Mighty Athena! How large are your fingers!

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: This is pea-soup, as exquisite as it is fine; Pallas the victorious goddess at Pylos is the one who crushed the peas herself.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Oh, Demos! the goddess watches over you; she is stretching forth over your head ... a stew-pan full of broth.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: And should we still be dwelling in this city without this protecting stew-pan?

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Here are some fish, given to you by her who is the terror of our foes.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: The daughter of the mightiest of the gods sends you this meat cooked in its own gravy, along with this dish of tripe and some paunch.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: That's to thank me for the peplus I offered to her; good.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: The goddess with the terrible plume invites you to eat this long cake; you will row the harder on it.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Take this also.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: And what shall I do with this tripe?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: She sends it you to belly out your galleys, for she is always showing her kindly anxiety for our fleet. Now drink this drink composed of three parts of water to two of wine.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Ah! what delicious wine, and how well it stands the water.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: The goddess who came from the head of Zeus mixed this liquor with her own hands.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Hold, here is a piece of good rich cake.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: But I offer you an entire cake.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: But you cannot offer him stewed hare as I do.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Ah! great gods! stewed hare! where shall I find it? Oh! brain of mine, devise some trick!

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Do you see this, you rogue?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: A fig for that! Here are some people coming to seek me. They are envoys, bearing sacks bulging with money.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.stage: Hearing money mentioned Cleon turns his head, and the Sausage-Seller seizes the opportunity to snatch away the stewed hare.
sp.p: Where, where, I say?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Bah! What's that to you? Will you not even now let the strangers alone? Dear Demos, do you see this stewed hare which I bring you?

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Ah! rascal! you have shamelessly robbed me.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: You have robbed too, you robbed the Laconians at Pylos.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Please tell me, how did you get the idea to filch it from him?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: The idea comes from the goddess; the theft is all my own.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: And I had taken such trouble to catch this hare and I was the one who had it cooked.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Get you gone! My thanks are only for him who served it.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Ah! wretch! you have beaten me in impudence!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Well then, Demos, say now, who has treated you best, you and your stomach? Decide!

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: How shall I act here so that the spectators shall approve my judgment?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I will tell you. Without saying anything, go and rummage through my basket, and then through the Paphlagonian's, and see what is in them; that's the best way to judge.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Let us see then, what is there in yours?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Why, it's empty, dear little father; I have brought everything to you.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: This is a basket devoted to the people.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Now hunt through the Paphlagonian's. Pause, as Demos does so Well?

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Oh! what a lot of good things! Why it's quite full! Oh! what a huge great part of this cake he kept for himself! He had only cut off the least little tiny piece for me.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: But this is what he has always done. Of everything he took, he only gave you the crumbs, and kept the bulk.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Oh! rascal! was this the way you robbed me? And I was loading you with chaplets and gifts!

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: I robbed for the public weal.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Give me back that crown; I shall give it to him.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Return it quick, quick, you gallows-bird.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: No, for the Pythian oracle has revealed to me the name of him who shall overthrow me.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: And that name was mine, nothing can be clearer.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Reply and I shall soon see whether you are indeed the man whom the god intended. Firstly, what school did you attend when a child?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: It was in the kitchens, where I was taught with cuffs and blows.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: What's that you say? aside Ah! this is truly what the oracle said. To the Sausage-Seller And what did you learn from the master of exercises?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I learnt to take a false oath without a smile, when I had stolen something.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Oh! Phoebus Apollo, god of Lycia! I am undone! To the Sausage-Seller And when you had become a man, what trade did you follow?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I sold sausages and did a bit of fornication.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Oh! my god! I am a lost man! Ah! still one slender hope remains.to the Sausage-Seller Tell me, was it on the market-place or near the gates that you sold your sausages?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Near the gates, in the market for salted goods.

sp.speaker: Cleon
sp.p: Alas! I see the prophecy of the god is verily come true. Alas! roll me home. I am a miserable ruined man. Farewell, my chaplet. 'Tis death to me to part with you. So you are to belong to another; 'tis certain he cannot be a greater thief, but perhaps he may be a luckier one.
sp.stage: He gives the chaplet to the Sausage-Seller.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Oh! Zeus, protector of Greece! 'tis to you I owe this victory!

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: Hail! illustrious conqueror, but forget not, that if you have become a great man, 'tis thanks to me; I ask but a little thing; appoint me secretary of the law-court in the room of Phanus.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: But what is your name then? Tell me.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: My name is Agoracritus, because I have always lived on the agora in the midst of lawsuits.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Well then, Agoracritus, I stand by you; as for the Paphlagonian, I hand him over to your mercy.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Demos, I will care for you to the best of my power, and all shall admit that no citizen is more devoted than I to this city of simpletons.

div.stage: They all enter the house of Demos.

sp.speaker: Chorus
sp.p: What fitter theme for our Muse, at the close as at the beginning of our work, than this, to sing the hero who drives his swift steeds down the arena? Why afflict Lysistratus with our satires on his poverty, and Thumantis, who has not so much as a lodging? He is dying of hunger and can be seen at Delphi, his face bathed in tears, clinging to your quiver, oh, Apollo! and supplicating you to take him out of his misery.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
Chorus
sp.p: At times a thought weighs on me at night; I wonder whence comes this fearful voracity of Cleonymus. 'Tis said that when dining with a rich host, he springs at the dishes with the gluttony of a wild beast and never leaves the bread-bin until his host seizes him round the knees, exclaiming, “Go, go, good gentleman, in mercy go, and spare my poor table!”

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: It is said that the triremes assembled in council and that the oldest spoke in these terms, “Are you ignorant, my sisters, of what is plotting in Athens? They say that a certain Hyperbolus, a bad citizen and an infamous scoundrel, asks for a hundred of us to take them to sea against Carthage.” All were indignant, and one of them, as yet a virgin, cried, “May god forbid that I should ever obey him! I would prefer to grow old in the harbor and be gnawed by worms. No! by the gods I swear it, Nauphante, daughter of Nauson, shall never bend to his law; that's as true as I am made of wood and pitch.
