If the Athenians vote for the proposal of Hyperbolus, let them! we will hoist full sail and seek refuge by the temple of Theseus or the shrine of the Eumenides. No! he shall not command us! No! he shall not play with the city to this extent! Let him sail by himself for Tartarus, if such please him, launching the boats in which he used to sell his lamps.”

div.stage: The Sausage-Seller comes out of the house of Demos, splendidly robed.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Maintain a holy silence! Keep your mouths from utterance! call no more witnesses; close these tribunals, which are the delight of this city, and gather at the theater to chant the Paean of thanksgiving to the gods for a fresh favour.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Oh! torch of sacred Athens, saviour of the Islands, what good tidings are we to celebrate by letting the blood of the victims flow in our market-places?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I have freshened Demos up somewhat on the stove and have turned his ugliness into beauty.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: I admire your inventive genius; but, where is he?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: He is living in ancient Athens, the city of the garlands of violets.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: How I should like to see him! What is his dress like, what his manner?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: He has once more become as he was in the days when he lived with Aristides and Miltiades. But you will judge for yourselves, for I hear the vestibule doors opening. Hail with your shouts of gladness the Athens of old, which now doth reappear to your gaze, admirable, worthy of the songs of the poets and the home of the illustrious Demos.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Oh! noble, brilliant Athens, whose brow is wreathed with violets, show us the sovereign master of this land and of all Greece.
sp.stage: Demos comes from his house, rejuvenated and joyous.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Lo! here he is coming with his hair held in place with a golden band and in all the glory of his old-world dress; perfumed with myrrh, he spreads around him not the odor of lawsuits, but that of peace.

sp.speaker: Leader of the Chorus
sp.p: Hail! King of Greece, we congratulate you upon the happiness you enjoy; it is worthy of this city, worthy of the glory of Marathon.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Come, Sausage-Seller, come, my best friend; see the service you have done me by freshening me up on your stove.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Ah! if you but remembered what you were formerly and what you did, you would for a certainty believe me to be a god.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: But what did I do? and how was I then?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Firstly, so soon as ever an orator declared in the Assembly, “Demos, I love you ardently; it is I alone who dream of you and watch over your interests”; at such an exordium you would look like a cock flapping his wings or a bull tossing his horns.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: What, I?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Then, after he had fooled you to the hilt, he would go.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: What! they would treat me so, and I never saw it?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: You knew only how to open and close your ears like a sunshade.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Was I then so stupid and such a dotard?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Worse than that; if one of two orators proposed to equip a fleet for war and the other suggested the use of the same sum for paying out to the citizens, it was the latter who always carried the day. Well! you droop your head! Why do you turn away your face?

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: I am blushing at my past errors.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Think no more of them; it's not you who are to blame, but those who cheated you in this sorry fashion. But, come, if some impudent lawyer dared to say, “Dicasts, you shall have no wheat unless you convict this accused man!” what would you do? Tell me.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: I would have him removed from the bar, I would bind Hyperbolus about his neck like a stone and would fling him into the Barathrum.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Well spoken! but what other measures do you wish to take?

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: First, as soon as ever a fleet returns to the harbor, I shall pay up the rowers in full.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: That will soothe many a worn and chafed bottom.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Further, the hoplite enrolled for military service shall not get transferred to another service through favour, but shall stick to that given him at the outset.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: This will strike the buckler of Cleonymus full in the center.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: None shall ascend the rostrum, unless his chin is bearded.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: What then will become of Clisthenes and of Strato?

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: I wish only to refer to those youths who loll about the perfume shops, babbling at random, “What a clever fellow is Phaeax! How cleverly he escaped death! how concise and convincing is his style! what phrases! how clear and to the point! how well he knows how to quell an interruption!”

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: I thought you were the lover of those fairies.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: The gods forefend it! and I will force all such fellows to go hunting instead of proposing decrees.

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: In that case, accept this folding-stool, and, to carry it, this well-grown, big-balled slave lad. Besides, you may put him to any other purpose you please.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Oh! I am happy indeed to find myself as I was of old!

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: Aye, you will deem yourself happy, when I have handed you the truce of thirty years. Truce! step forward!

div.stage: Enter Truce, in the form of a beautiful young girl, magnificently attired.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Great gods! how charming she is! Can I do with her as I wish? where did you discover her, pray?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: That Paphlagonian had kept her locked up in his house, so that you might not enjoy her. As for myself, I give her to you; take her with you into the country.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: And what punishment will you inflict upon this Paphlagonian, the cause of all my troubles?

sp.speaker: Sausage-Seller
sp.p: It will not be over-terrible. I condemn him to follow my old trade; posted near the gates, he must sell sausages of asses' and dogs' meat; perpetually drunk, he will exchange foul language with prostitutes and will drink nothing but the dirty water from the baths.

sp.speaker: Demos
sp.p: Well conceived! he is indeed fit to wrangle with harlots and bathmen; as for you, in return for so many blessings, I invite you to take the place at the Prytaneum which this rogue once occupied. Put on his frog-green mantle and follow me. As for the other, let them take him away; let him go sell his sausages in full view of the foreigners, whom he used formerly to insult so wantonly.
